Lessons.Title: Multi-step Conversion Problems: Customary Length
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 IM Grade5 U06:L07 solves customary length units across inches, feet and yards, using an open physical measurement card-sort and TWO original rectangular running-field contexts. One yard equals3 feet, one foot12 inches, one mile1760 yards=5280 feet.
Warm-up original source45×10=450,45×2=90,45×12=540,46×12=552; pupils use doubling and tenfold components rather than trying a new algorithm for12.

Activity1 source Customary Measurements card-sort gives source card images that are not independently readable from student HTML. Students categorize physical dimensions twice, match equal measures, then order groups in increasing physical length; previous self-authored sample2yd=6ft=72in remains optional, not official card deck.

Activity2 source field1 length90 yards, width42¼ yards, perimeter2×(90+42.25)=264.5yd. Six laps=1587yd, LESS than one mile1760yd by173yd, so original Priya claim that six laps exceed a mile is false. Field2 original408½ft long,240¼ft wide, perimeter1297.5ft; eight laps=10380ft still short of two miles10560ft, so NINE whole laps are required to reach at least two miles.

Previous fictional100×48.5yd or90×55yd figures are mathematically valid Edulytiks extensions, not source. Source cards, student unit explanations and original cool-down remain teacher reviewed; selected numeric Practice only covers exact bounded arithmetic.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: sort and compare inches, feet and yards, then solve multi-step customary-length stories involving a rectangular field's perimeter and a whole number of laps compared with a mile. The source first lets learners sort measurement cards by any justified grouping and then requires matching equivalent physical lengths.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: measure or describe a one-yard stick with three feet and36 inches. Explain why a number such as72 inches describes the same distance as6 feet or2 yards and why a larger printed count does not mean a longer object.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — first-party card equivalents: match 2 yards=6 feet=72 inches, 2 1/2 yards=7 1/2 feet=90 inches, and3 yards=9 feet=108 inches. Sort the representations both by unit form and by exact physical length, then order the groups from shortest to longest. Teacher reviews alternate valid classification criteria.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — perimeter and mile: original rectangular field100 yards long by48 1/2 yards wide has perimeter2×(100+48 1/2)=297 yards. Six laps equal1782 yards, which is22 yards MORE than one mile (1760 yards). For another field90 by55 yards, perimeter290 yards; twelve laps cover3480 yards, short of two miles (3520 yards), while thirteen cover3770, so13 full laps are required to reach at least two miles.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: the card-sort criteria, diagrams of a field and interpretation of a whole lap cannot be certified by a numeric converter; source asks students to critique a claim, state units and defend a minimum count. Original card images and protected teacher responses not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Customary length relations
KeyConcepts.Definition: One yard equals three feet equals36 inches; one mile equals5280 feet or1760 yards.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rectangular perimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two laps over each pair of perpendicular sides form a rectangle's perimeter.

KeyConcepts.Title: Minimum whole laps
KeyConcepts.Definition: For 'at least' a distance, use the smallest whole number of complete laps whose product meets the target.

Lessons.Title: Add and Subtract Fractions PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L08 permits adding/subtracting fractions with same or different denominators, encouraging visual representations and equivalent unit fractions before formalizing a single common-denominator algorithm.

Warm-up original Which One Doesn't Belong: fraction representations A–D show pictured number lines and equivalent shaded lengths. Source image B includes number lines in thirds and sixths, C represents two-thirds and eight-twelfths, but incomplete image data prevents reconstructing all A/D exact contents. Teacher reviews all original pictures and accepts multiple supported WODB reasons.

Activity1 original teacher-given cards for Fraction Sums and Differences ask students to sort twice under their own mathematical category choices. The original card deck is not fully encoded in teacher HTML; do not fabricate official expressions. First-party sample fraction cards may appear ONLY as Edulytiks independent extensions.

Activity2 original printed fractions are2/3+2/3=4/3=1⅓,2/3−1/6=4/6−1/6=3/6=1/2,2/3+1/2=4/6+3/6=7/6=1⅙. These support three different denominator relationships; learners explain equivalent units and their chosen diagrams.

Selected Practice tests exactly these three printed numerical values only; original WODB images, card sort and explanation need TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Source-gated publisher Cool-down not claimed replicated; independent Edulytiks teacher Cool-down clearly distinct.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: add and subtract fraction quantities when denominators match or differ by inventing categories for an expression-card sort, then using diagrams, equal parts or equivalent fractions in any mathematically defensible way. The source explicitly permits multiple grouping rationales and does not require formal common-denominator rules as the only entry point.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: compare one half with two fourths using a single fixed-unit tape. Both shade the same length and have different numerator/denominator pairs; explain why they can be combined after renaming one or both.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — category sort: first-party expressions 3/4+1/2,3/4+3/4,3/4−1/8,2/5+3/10 and5/6−1/3 may be grouped by same versus different denominators, by addition versus subtraction, or by whether the result exceeds one. At least two valid classification systems and student explanations are required.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — find three values: 3/4+3/4=6/4=1 1/2 by adding identical fourths; 3/4−1/8=6/8−1/8=5/8 by eighth strips; 3/4+1/2=3/4+2/4=5/4=1 1/4 by common quarters. Different number-line or tape-diagram strategies must refer to the same unit whole.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: the original task asks learners to explain their own sort, change categories and choose strategies. A single automated arithmetic answer cannot certify card sorting, drawn partitions, partner comparison or multiple valid methods.

Lessons.Title: Use Equivalent Expressions
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L09 asks pupils to add/subtract fractions by rewriting as equivalent expressions with a common denominator when one denominator is a multiple of the other; the source expects multiple valid calculation strategies and partner explanations.
Warm-up printed T/F1/4+2/4=3/4 TRUE;1/2+1/4=2/4 FALSE because3/4;3/4−1/2=2/4 FALSE because1/4. Teacher scores why fractions need same-sized units.

Activity1 Equal Sums ORIGINAL 2/3+10/12 =8/12+10/12=18/12=3/2=1½, or4/6+5/6=9/6=3/2. The book explicitly asks WHY all three forms are equivalent, not just numeric output; previous invented2/3+5/12 gives13/12 but is not the source original.
Activity2 Find Value of Difference original16/12−3/6=4/3−1/2=5/6, with students comparing methods and decomposing fractions as needed.

Optional Activity3 Grow Plants original Jada1¾in, Andre7/8in, difference7/8in; teacher reviews context and length units. Source drawing and original Cool-down remained teacher-scored/unverified where gated; independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down distinct.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: identify several equivalent fraction sums/differences and strategically choose a common denominator, sometimes simplifying before adding. The 2021 source asks why alternative expressions are equivalent, then compares different decompositions for differences and optionally a plant-growth story with unlike fractions.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: a fraction such as 3/4 can be described as6/8 or9/12 because the count and size of parts change together. Explain why multiplying just the numerator produces a different quantity.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — same sum with different units: find 2/3+5/12. Convert2/3=8/12 to obtain13/12=1 1/12. Alternatively work in sixths and twelfths as needed, showing that equivalent forms preserve the original total. Describe why twelfths are convenient without insisting they are the only denominator.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — subtract and compare: find 5/4−1/2 as5/4−2/4=3/4, or rewrite 5/4=15/12 and1/2=6/12 for9/12=3/4. A plant example using hypothetical growth1 5/8 inches versus3/4 inch gives a difference of7/8 inch; a student can add on or subtract after renaming.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: source requires matching equivalences, explaining numerator-and-denominator transformations, and comparing partner strategies. Numeric fractions alone do not prove the learner understood why a new expression is equivalent.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fraction identity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same nonzero integer preserves fraction value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choose a helpful common denominator
KeyConcepts.Definition: A denominator that both original denominators divide evenly allows comparison of same-sized parts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mixed fraction differences
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mixed fraction can be changed to an improper fraction or compared with another fraction by adding on.

Lessons.Title: All Sorts of Denominators
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L10 explains why multiplying two denominators always yields a COMMON DENOMINATOR while a smaller common multiple may be mathematically more efficient. Student strategies and representations remain flexible.

Warm-up How Many Do You See Fraction Sum uses publisher figure which is not independently reconstructed by plain source text. Teacher assesses fractions drawn and explains same whole; do not invent exact original shading.
Activity1 Different Denominators printed problems3/4+7/8=13/8=1⅝;3/4+4/6=17/12=1 5/12;3/4−2/5=7/20. Choose denominators8/12/20, explain how equivalent fractions preserve quantities.

Activity2 Multiply Denominators: Lin original2/5+4/9 uses common denominator45, correct18/45+20/45=38/45. Other source problems3/8+1/5=23/40,7/10−2/3=1/30,7/20+41/50=117/100=1 17/100,2/9−1/6=1/18. The product of denominators always works, but students compare practical smaller common denominator choices if available.

Previous invented3/8+2/5,2/3+5/9 values remain mathematically valid optional Edulytiks examples and NOT original source tasks. Exact selected questions cover source printed fraction values; original drawings, Lin's proof and teacher discussion remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: explain why multiplying two denominators always produces SOME common denominator, then choose a smaller or more useful common multiple when available. The source contrasts using a guaranteed product with spotting an easier common unit, and asks children to justify both the method and their actual sum/difference.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: compare the common denominator 24 for3/4+2/3 with the smaller denominator12. Both are mathematically sound, but 12 produces smaller equivalent numerators than24. Explain why multiplying4×3=12 always supplies a multiple of both.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — new sums: find3/8+2/5 using40ths, giving15/40+16/40=31/40. Find7/10−2/3 using30ths, giving21/30−20/30=1/30. Students can draw area bars, use multiplicative equivalence, or explain part counts.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — choose between denominators: 2/3+5/9 can use9ths to give6/9+5/9=11/9, or27ths to give18/27+15/27=33/27=11/9. Discuss why both work, and why the least common denominator is often more convenient while the denominator product is a guaranteed fallback.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: teacher reviews a proof of denominator product as a common multiple, correct equivalences and a rationale for choice. Merely outputting31/40 is a small algorithmic subskill of the original source task.

KeyConcepts.Title: Product denominator always works
KeyConcepts.Definition: For positive denominators b and d, bd is divisible by both b and d.

KeyConcepts.Title: Smaller common multiple can be simpler
KeyConcepts.Definition: A common denominator need not be the least, but smaller equivalent counts are often easier.

KeyConcepts.Title: Like-unit subtraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Common denominators let numerators count same-size parts.

Lessons.Title: Different Ways to Subtract
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 Grade5 U06:L11 compares different ways of subtracting unlike-denominator fractions including mixed numbers, with regrouping a whole into fractional parts or counting up. Student source explanations are assessed by teacher.
Warm-up original3+7/8=3 7/8,3−7/8=2 1/8,1 5/8+6/8=2 3/8 and1 5/8−6/8=7/8. Pupils reflect on full-part regrouping.

Activity1 original selects equivalent expressions to3 5/8: 20/8 is NOT equal (2.5), but2 13/8 and3 10/16 ARE equal. Source subtractions3 5/8−3/16=3 7/16,3 5/8−1 15/16=1 11/16,3 5/8−1 12/16=1 7/8. Teachers verify student's mixed-number interpretation.
Activity2 printed9 1/8−8 8/9=17/72,3 1/2−10/4=1,4 3/5−1 2/3=2 14/15. These include subtle unlike denominator comparisons and one mixed difference near zero requiring careful common parts.

Previous fictional4 1/4−2 5/6 remains optional Edulytiks exercise only; original publisher diagrams and written argument require teacher review. Selected choices cover fixed source values and error diagnosis.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: subtract unlike-denominator mixed numbers and select among decomposition, regrouping and adding-on strategies, explaining why an equivalent mixed-number form can make a tricky fractional subtraction possible. The source deliberately uses fractions close to a whole and has students compare work in a gallery display.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: rename 4 1/4 as3 5/4 and as17/4; all are the same amount, but the second mixed expression permits subtracting a larger fractional part. Identify when borrowing one whole is useful.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — justify regrouping: calculate4 1/4−2 5/6. Rewrite4 1/4 as3 15/12, because4 1/4=3+15/12; 2 5/6=2+10/12. Subtract corresponding whole and twelfth parts to yield1+5/12=1 5/12. Compare to directly computing17/4−17/6=17/12. The original whole stays fixed.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — count up for close mixed numbers: 5 1/8−4 7/8 can be found by adding1/8 to4 7/8 to get5, then1/8 more to5 1/8, total1/4. Another 3 2/3−1 5/6 can be found with sixths: 22/6−11/6=11/6=1 5/6. Ask learners which approach is clearest and why.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: source asks for selecting equivalences, a valid diagram, a reasoned method choice, and comparison of gallery displays; a numeric answer does not verify those student-generated reasoning tasks. Protected source graphics and gated response not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Regroup one whole in a mixed number
KeyConcepts.Definition: One whole can be exchanged for denominator-many fractional pieces to make a subtraction possible.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common units in mixed difference
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rewrite fractions as equal-sized parts before subtracting.

KeyConcepts.Title: Adding on
KeyConcepts.Definition: The gap between near-whole mixed numbers can be counted by short forward steps.
